opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the central tensions right now, and it shows up especially clearly when you move from the digital world into the physical world, which is where I spend most of my time.

Large language models gained their generality by training on an enormous amount of internet data. They learned a very broad statistical picture of human language and knowledge, which is why they can talk about almost anything. But generality in that sense isn't the same as reliability. A model can be broadly competent and still be wrong in ways that are hard to predict. It hallucinates, it's confidently imprecise, and in many tasks being 90% right is fine. If you're writing an email or brainstorming, an occasional mistake costs very little.

When you put that intelligence into a robot, the standard changes completely. If a robot grasps something correctly 90% of the time, the other 10% means dropping a cup, breaking something, or failing a task in a factory. Physical tasks are often long-horizon, so small error rates compound across many steps. In the physical world, accuracy isn't a nice-to-have. It's the precondition for anyone actually deploying the system.

So I don't think generality and accuracy are fundamentally opposed, but they come from different sources. Generality comes from scale and diversity of data. Accuracy, especially in embodied settings, comes from grounding: closed-loop feedback, data that really covers the physical interactions you care about, and often some structure or verification in the system, not just one big model guessing end to end.

My view is that the path forward is layered. You use the broad, general model for high-level understanding: what the person wants, what the scene means, what the plan should be. Then, for the parts where precision matters, like low-level control and contact-rich manipulation, you need models trained on large amounts of high-quality physical data, much of it from simulation and synthetic generation, because real-world robot data is so expensive to collect. Simulation lets you cover the long tail of situations, and that is where accuracy comes from.

There's also an intermediate stage I think people sometimes skip over. Before you get a truly general robot, you get robots that are very accurate in a few specific scenarios: retail, pharmacies, factory logistics. That's not a retreat from generality. It's how you build the data flywheel. You deploy where you can be reliable, you collect real data, and you gradually expand the boundary. I believe generality will be earned through accuracy, scenario by scenario, rather than the other way around.

r001.rationale: The response says LLMs gained broad generality through training on enormous amounts of internet data, but it does not state that they achieve it in a single step.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the first thing to say is that these two things are often framed as a trade-off, and I don't think that framing is quite right, at least not in the simple way people imagine.

The intuition people have is something like: a model that does everything will be mediocre at everything, and a model that does one thing will be excellent at that one thing. That comes from an older era of machine learning, where you trained a classifier for one task on one dataset, and generality really did cost you. If you wanted a model to handle more tasks, you usually gave something up on each individual task.

What large language models showed is that, within a certain range, generality and accuracy actually move together. When you train on enormous amounts of diverse data, the model learns representations that transfer. Being good at code helps with reasoning. Being good at reasoning helps with math. Having read a lot of law and a lot of medicine helps the model understand a question that sits between those fields. So the breadth is not a tax on the accuracy; in many cases it's the source of the accuracy. A model that only ever saw medical text would be worse at medicine than a model that saw medical text plus everything else, which is a slightly counterintuitive result if you come from the old paradigm.

But I'd add two caveats.

The first is that generality defines the ceiling, not the floor. A general model can reach very high accuracy on a given domain, but it doesn't automatically do so. The last stretch, going from "very good" to "reliable enough for a doctor or a lawyer or an engineer to actually depend on," usually requires domain-specific work: curated data, evaluation that reflects how experts actually judge quality, feedback from people who know the field. So in practice, you still see specialization, but it's specialization on top of a general base rather than instead of it.

The second caveat is about what we mean by accuracy. For a narrow model, accuracy is a single number on a benchmark. For a general model, the hard problem isn't average accuracy; it's knowing where the model is accurate and where it isn't. The same model can be excellent at one question and confidently wrong on a neighboring question, and from the outside they look identical. So I actually think the more important axis is not generality versus accuracy, but generality versus calibration. Can the model tell you when it's on solid ground and when it's guessing? That's the thing that determines whether the generality is usable.

So my short answer would be: generality has mostly been a driver of accuracy rather than its enemy, but it moves the real problem. The problem is no longer "can it do the task," it's "do we know when to trust it." And that second problem is, I think, where a lot of the interesting work over the next few years will be.

r001.rationale: The response describes broad capabilities arising from training on diverse data, but does not state that LLMs achieve high generality in a single step.

astra-6.text:
I think generality and accuracy are related, but they’re not the same thing. A model can handle a very wide range of questions without being reliably correct on every one of them. And a system can be highly accurate within a narrow domain while struggling as soon as you step outside it.

The interesting question is whether generality helps you achieve accuracy. I think it can: a broad foundation gives a model the ability to connect ideas, interpret unfamiliar questions, and apply knowledge across tasks. But that alone doesn’t guarantee a correct answer. You still need ways to check evidence, verify results, and recognize when there isn’t enough information.

So I wouldn’t frame this as choosing one over the other. Generality expands what a model can attempt; accuracy determines how much we can trust what it produces. For practical applications, we need both—and we need the model to communicate its limits.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses generality as broad task coverage, but does not state that large language models achieve a high degree of generality in a single step.

sol-6.1.text:
I think generality and accuracy are related, but one doesn’t automatically imply the other. A large language model can discuss many subjects fluently, yet still make mistakes on a specific question. Breadth of coverage is different from reliability.

At the same time, generality can help accuracy. The ability to connect ideas across domains and use context can help a model solve problems that a narrowly specialized system might struggle with. So I wouldn’t describe this as a simple trade-off.

The key is what we mean by accuracy and how we measure it. For brainstorming, a useful range of possibilities may be enough. For a medical or financial question, a plausible answer isn’t enough—you need evidence, verification, and appropriate uncertainty. The goal is to preserve broad capability while making the model reliable on the particular task, including knowing when it doesn’t have enough information to answer.

r001.rationale: The response describes broad subject coverage, but does not state that large language models achieve a high degree of generality in a single step.
